turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Yeah, thank you. Um, well, what brings me in... it's kind of hard to explain where it starts, but I just haven't been right lately. I keep having this incredibly heavy feeling that I've just completely let my family down. We took on this mortgage recently—it was supposed to be a good thing, you know, getting a little more space for us—but I don't know why I thought I could handle it. I mean, I work at a restaurant waiting tables, and the math just... it keeps me up at night. I feel like I've trapped them. 

And it's bleeding into absolutely everything else. Like, at work, I'll make a tiny mistake. The other day I forgot to ring in a side salad for a table, or I'll drop a glass, just simple mistakes anyone could make, right? But for me, it doesn't feel simple anymore. It feels like this massive, glaring proof that I'm just completely useless. I literally stand there and spiral, thinking about how I'm a failure and how I honestly deserve whatever bad things happen to me. Like, if I get fired or if we end up losing the house, it's exactly what I deserve because I'm just not good enough to provide for them. It's just this constant, crushing guilt, and I can't seem to stop my brain from going over and over every little thing I do wrong, and I just... I don't know how to turn it off.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient mentions that worrying about the math for their mortgage keeps them up at night, indicating a disturbance in sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S030: The patient expresses constant, crushing guilt, feelings of being completely useless, and a belief that they are a failure who deserves bad things.

turns.doctor_question: During this time, have you lost interest or pleasure in doing the things you usually enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I mean... I don't really do much of anything I used to enjoy anyway, but even if I try, it's just... it's not the same. It's hard to explain, but most days there's just this incredibly heavy, almost completely empty feeling right here in my chest. It just sits there. 

Like, take work for example. I used to actually kind of like the hustle and bustle of the restaurant, you know? Chatting with the regulars, joking around with the kitchen staff, that sort of thing. But lately, I'm just going through the motions. I'm carrying plates back and forth, weaving through the tables, refilling drinks, and I'm smiling at the customers because, well, as a waiter you're supposed to smile. You have to put on that friendly face if you want to make any tips to pay that mortgage I was talking about. But I'm only doing it because I'm supposed to, not because I feel anything good. 

I'm definitely not smiling because I'm happy to be there. I'm just mechanically putting one foot in front of the other. And it's like that at home, too. I used to like watching a baseball game or just messing around in the yard, but now... I just feel so hollowed out. Like all the color is just drained out of everything. I wake up with that empty feeling, I take it to work with me, I fake my way through my shift, and I bring it right back home. I just can't seem to shake it or find any actual joy in anything I'm doing anymore, no matter how hard I try to force it.

turns.doctor_question: About how long have you been experiencing this heavy, empty feeling?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... I mean, it's hard to pinpoint the exact day or anything, because it kind of sneaks up on you, you know? It's not like you wake up one Tuesday and suddenly everything is gray. It's more like... like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it at first, but then one day you're driving and the car is pulling hard to one side and you realize, wow, I've been riding on the rim for a while. 

But if I really think about when that heavy, guilty feeling—that total emptiness—really settled in and just refused to leave... I'd say it's been going on for about a year and two months now. Yeah, about 14 months. Because I remember it was right around the time we were first starting to seriously look at houses, before we even signed any papers for the mortgage. I remember standing in the kitchen of our old apartment, looking at the water stain on the ceiling that the landlord would never fix, and just feeling this overwhelming sense of dread wash over me. And it just... it hasn't stopped since then. It's been this constant companion, this shadow that just follows me from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep, for over a year now. Just... a year and two months of feeling completely hollowed out and guilty for everything.

turns.doctor_question: Before this started about 14 months ago, had you ever experienced another period in your life where you felt this down or empty?
turns.patient_response:
No, I really don't think so. I mean, I've tried to think back on my life, you know, trying to figure out if I've always been like this and just didn't notice, or if this is something completely new. And honestly, looking back, I don't remember ever feeling this... this profound sense of just being completely hollowed out. 

I mean, sure, I had bad days before. Everyone has bad days, right? Like when I was in college—I went for a couple of years before I dropped out, mostly just general ed stuff, couldn't figure out what I wanted to do—and I remember being stressed about finals, or being bummed out when a relationship ended. There was this one girl I dated my sophomore year, and when we broke up, I was definitely sad for a few weeks. I listened to a lot of depressing music and didn't want to hang out with my friends. But that felt normal, you know? It felt like a reaction to something that actually happened. It wasn't this... this heavy, suffocating blanket that just covers everything, even the good stuff. 

And even working at the restaurant over the years. I've been waiting tables for a long time, and there are definitely shifts that just beat you down. You get a bad tip, or a customer yells at you over something you can't control, or the kitchen is backed up and you're the one taking the heat. You go home tired and frustrated. But I always bounced back. I'd wake up the next day, have a cup of coffee, and feel okay again. I never carried that feeling with me for weeks and months on end like I do now. So, no, before this started 14 months ago, I can honestly say I've never experienced anything even close to this level of just... total emptiness and guilt. It's completely new, and it's just exhausting.

turns.doctor_question: With everything feeling so heavy and exhausting, have you had any thoughts of wanting to end your life, or feeling like you'd be better off dead?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... I wouldn't say I have a plan, you know? Like, I'm not sitting around trying to figure out how to do it or anything like that. I haven't gone out and bought anything, I haven't written any notes. It's not like a concrete plan where I'm actively trying to end things. But... it's just... it's the weight of it all, you know? It's so incredibly heavy. 

Sometimes, especially when I'm lying awake in bed... like, say I have an early shift at the restaurant. I have to be there by 9:00 AM to help set up the dining room, roll silverware, get the stations ready before the lunch rush hits. And I'll just be lying there in the dark at, like, 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, staring at the ceiling, listening to the hum of the refrigerator or whatever, and I just feel this crushing sense of... of just failing at everything. Failing at the mortgage, failing at being a functional person, just... failing. 

And in those moments, when it's so quiet and the guilt is just eating away at me, I do have these thoughts. I catch myself thinking... man, it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. If I could just drift off and not have to open my eyes and face it all again. Not have to put on that fake smile, not have to carry the plates, not have to feel this emptiness every single second of the day. It's not that I want to violently hurt myself, it's more like... I just want the struggle to stop. I just want to stop feeling like a burden and a failure. So, yeah, I guess I do think about it being easier if I just wasn't here anymore, just to get some relief from this constant, heavy feeling that I can't seem to shake.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period in your life where you felt the opposite—extremely energized, 'on top of the world,' or like you didn't need to sleep?
turns.patient_response:
No, never. I mean, I've never felt anything like that. The idea of feeling "on top of the world" just seems so foreign to me right now, but even looking back, before all this started, I don't think I ever had a time like that. I know some people get really hyped up, you know? Like they have all this energy and they're bouncing off the walls and getting a million things done. I had a roommate once, back when I was taking those college classes, who would pull all-nighters right before midterms and he'd just be wired, cleaning the whole apartment at 4 AM and talking a mile a minute. 

But me? I've always been pretty even-keeled, I guess. Well, before this last year and a half, anyway. I've always needed my sleep. If I don't get at least seven or eight hours, I'm just dragging the next day, especially at the restaurant. You can't be on your feet for an eight-hour shift, carrying heavy trays and dealing with people, if you haven't slept. So the idea of not needing sleep... no, that's never been me. I've never had a period where I felt like I had superpowers or endless energy or anything even close to that. It's always just been, you know, normal energy levels. And now, of course, it's just zero energy, all the time. But even before the emptiness set in, I was never the type to be overly energized or feeling invincible. Just... normal, I guess.

turns.doctor_question: Have you heard any voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?
turns.patient_response:
Well, actually... yeah. It’s kind of strange that you ask that, because I’ve been trying to figure out if my mind is just playing tricks on me because I'm so tired, or what. 

You know, at the restaurant, when I’m on the closing shift... usually that means the kitchen staff has already packed up and gone home, and it's just me out in the dining room and maybe the manager doing the drawer in the back office. I have to stay to do the final wipe-down of the booths, sweep the floor, and make sure all the salt and pepper shakers are topped off for the morning crew—because if they aren't, the morning manager will absolutely leave a nasty note about it. Once the overhead music gets turned off, the place gets incredibly quiet, just the hum of the ice machine. And lately, when I’m just standing there wiping a table or rolling the last of the napkins, I’ll hear this... this really low voice. 

Sometimes it just says my name, really quietly. But other times, it whispers that I’m going to lose everything. 

And it’s not just at work, either. It happens at home, too. When I’m sitting alone in the condo... I spend a lot of time just sitting on the couch these days, not even with the TV on, just sitting there in the silence because I don't have the energy to do anything else. And out of nowhere, I'll hear that same low whisper. "You're going to lose everything." 

It’s so clear. It doesn't sound like a thought inside my head, if that makes sense? It sounds physical. It sounds so real, like someone is standing right over my shoulder, right behind the couch, that I actually stop what I'm doing and turn around to check. I'll physically spin around, expecting to see someone standing there. At work, I've even called out, like, "Hey, Dave, did you say something?" thinking the manager stepped out of the office. But there’s never anyone there. It’s just me. And it really shakes me up, because it sounds so incredibly real, and it's whispering the exact things I'm already so terrified of with the mortgage and everything. I just... I turn around every time, because you can't *not* look when it sounds like someone is right there in the room with you.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing a clear, physical-sounding voice whispering their name or negative statements when no one else is present.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient mentions being 'so tired' and sitting in silence because they 'don't have the energy to do anything else'.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start hearing those whispers?
turns.patient_response:
Gosh, let me think about the exact timeline. It’s been... well, it’s been a while now. I’d say it’s been about a year and four months. I remember because it was right around the time the restaurant rolled out the new seasonal menu, and I was already stressed about memorizing all the new ingredients and the new wine pairings they expected us to upsell. That’s when the whispers really started to become a regular thing. 

But you know, it’s actually not just the whispers, either. For that entire time—that whole year and four months—I’ve also had this really intense, fixed fear that I’m being watched. It’s like this heavy, suffocating blanket over me. I’ll be in my condo, right? The blinds are completely shut, the deadbolt is locked, the chain is on the door, and I’m just sitting on the couch, and I will get this overwhelming, absolute certainty that there are eyes on me. Like someone is studying my every single move from somewhere just out of sight. I've even checked the air vents a few times because the feeling is just so strong. 

And it happens at work, too. I’ll be punching an order into the computer system, just tapping the screen for a medium-rare steak or putting in a substitution for a side salad, and the hair on the back of my neck will just stand straight up. I’ll whip around, expecting a customer or the manager to be staring daggers at me from across the dining room, but everyone is just going about their business, totally ignoring me. So it’s both of those things together, really—the whispering and that constant, terrifying feeling of being watched. They both started right around that same time, a year and four months ago, and they just haven't let up since. It just wears you down, constantly feeling like you have to look over your shoulder while you're already carrying all this other weight.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes an intense, fixed fear and absolute certainty of being watched, leading to checking air vents, which indicates persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms hearing whispers regularly for the past year and four months, indicating auditory hallucinations.

turns.patient_response:
It’s funny you ask about that specific timeframe, because I’ve actually thought about that a lot, trying to make sense of it all. You’d think that hearing things or feeling like you're being watched would only happen when your mood is at its absolute lowest, right? But... no, actually, that wasn't how it happened. 

There was actually this stretch of time back then, probably for several weeks or so, where my mood really wasn't especially depressed at all. I mean, I wasn't jumping for joy or anything, but I wasn't in that dark, heavy, empty place that I've been stuck in lately. I was actually getting through work so much better during those weeks. I was handling the dinner rushes fine, I was remembering all the new seasonal specials without any issues, chatting with my regulars, getting my side-work done quickly... I just felt pretty okay, emotionally speaking. My energy was normal, my mood was normal. 

But the weird thing is, even during those several weeks when I wasn't feeling depressed, the other stuff was definitely still happening. I’d be at home, sitting at my little kitchen table at the condo, just trying to sort through my mortgage paperwork. I like to keep all my statements and bills in this blue binder, you know, just to stay organized because the condo fees and the mortgage rate adjustments can get really complicated if you don't stay on top of them. And I’d be sitting there with my calculator, feeling totally fine emotionally, not sad or drained or anything, and I would still hear that whispering. Just... right there in the room with me. 

And that feeling of being watched didn't go away either. It was so intense, especially while I was looking over those mortgage documents. I’d be holding a bank statement, just doing basic math, and the hairs on my arms would stand straight up because I just felt this absolute certainty that someone was watching me read it. I'd keep looking over my shoulder at the hallway. So, yeah, even when my mood was totally fine and I was functioning perfectly well at work for those few weeks, that whispering at the condo and that feeling of eyes on me while I did my paperwork... they were definitely still there. It didn't seem to matter that I wasn't feeling depressed yet.
